analysis.note: Relative pronoun; printed as ya before enam by external sandhi, but the pausal form is yaḥ.

Enclitic accusative singular masculine form referring, per the commentary, to the prakṛta dehin, the ātman under discussion. Revised from enad to etad after the verifier rejected enad as deriving enadam.

Predicative accusative with enam: ‘as the slayer/agent of killing.’ Verifier note: I retain hantṛ, since hantāram is the standard masculine accusative singular of the agent noun hantṛ, with strong stem hantār-; the verifier’s hantaram reflects a non-agent/weak ṛ-stem treatment, not the intended form here.
Relative pronoun; yaḥ + ca is printed yaś ca.
Printed merged with following enam as cainaṃ = ca + enam.
Second occurrence, again referring to the self; printed merged with ca as cainaṃ. Revised from enad to etad after the verifier rejected enad as deriving enadam.
Ātmanepada form with active sense: ‘thinks, supposes.’
Past passive participial adjective from √han, agreeing predicatively with enam: ‘slain/killed.’
Dual masculine because it refers back to the two relative subjects yaḥ ... yaś ca.
Correlative to the two yaḥ-clauses: ‘those two.’
Pausal vijānītaḥ; visarga-sandhi before na gives printed vijānīto.
Printed together with following ayam as nāyaṃ = na + ayam.
Refers to the self; printed together with preceding na as nāyaṃ.
Active: ‘kills/slays’; the commentary denies agency in the self.
Passive: ‘is killed/slain’; the commentary glosses this as not being the karma, the object/patient of the killing-action.

justifications.decision: Translate the object as ‘this embodied self (dehin/ātman)’ and the later subject as ‘this self.’
justifications.chosen: enam/ayam refer to the embodied self, the ātman, not to the physical body as such.

evidence.quote: ya enaṃ prakṛtaṃ dehinaṃ vetti vijānāti
evidence.translation: ‘Who knows this, the embodied one under discussion.’

evidence.quote: tau ubhau na vijānītaḥ na jñātavantau avivekena ātmānam
evidence.translation: ‘Those two both do not know—have not known, through non-discrimination—the self.’
‘Because this self does not kill’ (the plaintext prints atmā, understood as ātmā).

justifications.decision: Render ya enaṃ vetti hantāram as ‘whoever takes this self to be the slayer’ and yaś cainaṃ manyate hatam as ‘whoever thinks this self slain.’
options_considered: hantāram as an ordinary object, ‘knows the killer’
hantāram/hatam as predicative accusatives applied to enam
hanyate as middle active rather than passive
justifications.chosen: hantāram is a predicative accusative meaning the agent of the killing-action; hatam is the corresponding patient/object of that action.

evidence.quote: ya enaṃ prakṛtaṃ dehinaṃ vetti vijānāti hantāraṃ hanana-kriyāyāḥ kartāraṃ ya ca enam anyo manyate hataṃ deha-hananena hato 'ham iti hanana-kriyāyāḥ karma-bhūtam
evidence.translation: ‘Who knows this embodied one under discussion, i.e. knows it as the killer, the agent of the act of killing; and another who thinks this to be killed—“I am killed” by the killing of the body—as become the object of the act of killing.’

evidence.quote: na ayam atmā hanti na hanana-kriyāyāḥ kartā bhavati, na ca hanyate na ca karma bhavatīty arthaḥ
evidence.translation: ‘This self does not kill, does not become the agent of the act of killing; nor is it killed, nor does it become the object.’

justifications.decision: Translate ubhau tau na vijānītaḥ as ‘both of those two do not understand,’ not as a mere absence of information about killing.
options_considered: ‘both do not know’ with no specified object
‘both do not know the act of killing’
‘both fail to know the self’s true nature’
justifications.chosen: na vijānītaḥ means that the two do not truly know the self’s nature.

evidence.quote: tau ubhau na vijānītaḥ na jñātavantau avivekena ātmānam
evidence.translation: ‘Those two both do not know—have not known, through non-discrimination—the self.’

evidence.quote: hantā ahaṃ, hato 'smy aham iti deha-hananena ātmānam ahaṃ pratyaya-viṣayaṃ yau vijānītaḥ tau ātma-svarūpānabhijñau ity arthaḥ
evidence.translation: ‘Those two who know the self, the object of the “I”-notion, as “I am the killer” or “I am killed” through the killing of the body are ignorant of the self’s own nature—this is the meaning.’

justifications.decision: Use a colon/causal sense in translation: their view is ignorance, for this self neither slays nor is slain.
options_considered: final pāda as a merely coordinate assertion
final pāda as causal/explanatory of the ignorance just stated
justifications.chosen: The last half states the reason: the self neither acts as killer nor undergoes being killed, because it is changeless.

evidence.quote: yasmāt na ayam atmā hanti na hanana-kriyāyāḥ kartā bhavati, na ca hanyate na ca karma bhavatīty arthaḥ, avikriyatvāt
evidence.translation: ‘Because this self does not kill, does not become the agent of the act of killing; nor is it killed, nor does it become the object—because of being changeless.’

justifications.decision: Render ubhau tau explicitly as ‘both of those two.’
options_considered: ubhau tau as a loose emphatic ‘both’
ubhau tau as the correlative pair answering yaḥ ... yaś ca
justifications.chosen: ubhau tau resumes the two relative clauses, the one who takes the self as killer and the one who takes it as killed.

evidence.translation: ‘The two who so know are ignorant of the self’s own nature.’

translation:
Whoever takes this embodied self (dehin/ātman) to be the slayer,
and whoever thinks this self slain—
both of those two do not understand:
this self neither slays nor is slain.
one_shot_delta: Without the bhāṣya one might take enam as the body or a person in general; Śaṅkara identifies it as the dehin/ātman under discussion.
A commentary-blind version might render vetti as straightforward true knowledge (‘knows him to be the killer’), whereas Śaṅkara says both cognizers are avivekin and ignorant of the self’s nature.
One might miss the agent/patient analysis: hantāram is ‘agent of the killing-action’ and hatam/hanyate is ‘object/patient of that action,’ both explicitly denied of the self.
One might translate the last half as merely another assertion; Śaṅkara marks it with yasmāt and explains it through avikriyatva, making it the reason the two views are ignorance.
analyzer_disagreements: enam (both occurrences): ByT5 tags lemma enad; I revise to etad because the verifier rejects enad as a stem, deriving enadam. The syntactic role and referent are unchanged: masculine accusative singular referring to the self under discussion.
ubhau: the analyzer gave lemma ubh; I record the nominal/pronominal stem ubha, masculine nominative dual, since it agrees with tau and refers to the two masculine yaḥ-subjects.
vijānītaḥ: the analyzer’s prefixed lemma vijñā is decomposed as required into bare root jñā with prefix vi; tense/person/number are otherwise retained.
hatam: the analyzer lemmatized the form to root han as a participial form; for a nominal word-analysis I record the actual participial stem hata, masculine accusative singular.
open_questions: Line 4 prints atmā; I have treated this as ātmā, a likely plaintext or editional typo, because the same commentarial explanation uses ātmānam in lines 2–3 and ātmeti in line 5.
